title: Verification and Falsification
welcome_lead: Enter the twentieth-century debate over whether religious sentences mean anything at all.
meta_desc: A-Level OCR Religious Studies adventure on logical positivism, Ayer's verificationism, Flew's falsification challenge, and replies.
final_note: You have followed the verification and falsification challenges to religious meaning and the principal Christian replies.

concepts.def: A statement is meaningful only if analytic or empirically verifiable.
Requires that some observations be relevant.
A genuine assertion must rule out some possible state of affairs.
Hick's claim that religious statements are in principle verifiable after death.

walkthroughs.body_html: A. J. Ayer's Language, Truth and Logic (1936) imported Vienna Circle verificationism into British philosophy. Genuine factual claims are analytic or empirically verifiable. 'God exists', 'stealing is wrong' and 'this is beautiful' fail and are 'literally nonsense'. Ayer later admitted (Introduction to second edition, 1946) that his strong form was too restrictive; he weakened it but the principle itself faced self-refutation worries.

Antony Flew's Theology and Falsification (1950) adapted John Wisdom's parable. Two explorers find a clearing; one believes a gardener tends it. As experiments fail, the believer qualifies endlessly: 'an invisible, intangible, eternally elusive gardener'. The original assertion has died 'the death of a thousand qualifications'. To assert is to deny something.

John Hick's parable of the Celestial City: travellers disagree about the road's destination, but the matter will be settled on arrival. Religious assertions are in principle verifiable post-mortem and so meaningful. R. M. Hare proposed bliks - unfalsifiable but action-guiding views, illustrated by the paranoid student convinced his dons want to kill him. Mitchell's partisan parable defends religious belief as cognitive assertion held under strain.
